title: Short Stuff: Aztec Death Whistle
summary: Short Stuff episode on the Aztec death whistle. The hosts describe a late-1990s excavation of an Aztec temple dedicated to the wind god Ehecatl in Mexico City, where a beheaded young male was found squatting at the base of the stairway holding two small whistles engraved with a skull. The whistles are interpreted as symbolizing the combination of the gods Mictlantecuhtli (death/underworld) and Ehecatl (wind). Archaeologist Arne Both examined the whistles, used CT scans, and built larger replicas; he found they are air spring whistles, which the hosts say the Maya developed around 700–800 CE. The hosts discuss the Codex Borgia as evidence for the god pairing and for wind imagery tied to the afterlife journey, and the festival Toxcatl honoring Tezcatlipoca. They conclude the whistles were likely ritual instruments tied to guiding souls through the underworld rather than battle weapons, and note that replicas sound underwhelming. Hosts also joke about mispronunciations in online videos.

segments.title: Opening banter and Mexico City
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the Aztec death whistle topic and mention the ruins under Mexico City, where a temple to the Aztec wind god was excavated in the late 1990s. They praise the Anthropology Museum in Mexico City.

segments.title: The beheaded man and the skull whistles
segments.summary: A beheaded young male was found at a temple base holding two small whistles engraved with skulls. The hosts say the whistles combine the gods of death and wind. The hosts also joke about mispronounced Nahuatl names in online videos.

segments.title: Arne Both and the first playing of the whistles
segments.summary: Music archaeologist Arne Both is introduced as the researcher who studied and first played the whistles, finding them underwhelming in sound. He used CT scans and built larger replicas.

segments.title: Air spring whistle mechanism
segments.summary: Both found the whistles are air spring whistles, which the Maya developed around 700 to 800 CE. Air blown through an intake tube reacts with the air spring in a chamber to distort the sound.

segments.title: Codex Borgia and the wind god pairing
segments.summary: The Codex Borgia shows the gods Ehecatl and Mictlantecuhtli back to back, guarding the underworld together. The hosts relate the pairing to life and death and to the wind-driven journey through the afterlife, which takes nine years.

segments.title: Ritual interpretation of the whistles
segments.summary: Obsidian blades and a ceramic bowl were found beside the body. Hosts conclude the whistles were ritual instruments used to help souls cross the underworld wind field, not battle weapons.

segments.title: Toxcatl festival and Lewis Spence
segments.summary: The hosts mention the Toxcatl festival honoring Tezcatlipoca. They quote folklorist Lewis Spence's 1913 description of a whistle imitating the night wind during the festival.

segments.title: Replica sound and battle use
segments.summary: Hosts describe videos of musicians playing death whistles and explain that large replicas do not sound like the originals. They say the whistles were probably not used in battle, unlike conch shells and drums.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts wrap up the short stuff segment and close with the standard iHeartRadio production credit.
